div.head: Organizational Structure of the SWAP Team
div.p: The primary responsibility for developing the Mississippi SWAP was given to the MMNS which functions as the MDWFP's non-game wildlife program and includes the MNHP. Similar to the process used to develop the previous SWAPs, two committees (Technical and Core Committees) and a group of wildlife experts and stakeholders were engaged to help revise and update the SWAP. For a full list of committee members and advisors, see Appendix 1. Each committee is described below.

The SWAP Technical Committee was composed of MDWFP's wildlife, fisheries, private lands, and museum biologists. They gathered and analyzed information needed to identify Mississippi's species and habitats, threats/limiting factors and potential conservation actions. They met monthly or as needed over a period of three years (2023 -2025), and significant correspondence and work occurred between meetings. They also coordinated their efforts with expert advisors, tribal representatives, and stakeholders composed of scientists in the state and region with expertise on the SGCN, and who provided additional input on species, habitats, threats and conservation actions. These experts also gave feedback individually to members of the Technical Committee on an as needed basis.

A Core Committee of SWAP state coordinators worked to ensure overall coordination of plan development and incorporation of the eight required elements. They approved plan formatting, plans for stakeholder and public involvement, plan review and revision and the agency approval process. They met regularly and communicated on an as needed basis through email and online meetings.

div.head: Stakeholder and Public Input
div.p: Representatives from natural resources agencies, conservation organizations, agriculture and forest products industries, technical experts, conservation educators and academics as well as individuals and additional MDWFP district and other staff were invited via email or personal contact to participate in the original plan development and in the review and update of the Mississippi SWAP. During the revision of the SWAP, these stakeholders communicated primarily via email, and through individual and small group meetings and submitted comments through the SWAP page on the MDWFP website. Their role was to provide input and advice during the SWAP update process, recommend existing plans or strategies for incorporation, and to review and comment on draft chapters and elements of the SWAP as they were developed prior to submission to the USFWS.

Several stakeholders representing public agencies, non-government organizations, tribal interests and individuals provided comments which were considered by the Technical Committee and incorporated into this revised plan throughout the three year process of updating the SGCN, habitat descriptions, threats, actions and other elements. In addition to the assistance solicited from members of the committees, experts and stakeholders, public input was invited through the MDWFP website and social media. A Mississippi SWAP page on the MDWFP website was developed in 2023 and plan elements were posted and announced as they were updated. The website was the primary method of providing SWAP revisions to the public and stakeholders for additional review and comments and included a direct link to email for feedback. The site will remain active as the 2025 SWAP is implemented and additional planning iterations are developed. More details and a summary of stakeholder, agency, tribal and public participation and outreach is in Appendix 1 and 2.

div.head: Coordination with Other Agencies
div.p: Development of this document was accomplished in coordination with several public wildlife agencies, universities, conservation organizations and land managers in Mississippi and in the Southeast U.S. This coordination was ensured by inclusion of representatives of these agencies and organizations serving as advisors, experts, through individual briefings and presentations and through contact with the Technical Committee. Conservation planning documents and tools provided by other agencies were gathered and incorporated into the SWAP where possible. Other interested parties also contributed to the process through comments via the MDWFP website or during one on one meetings, or during professional meetings, trainings and conferences related to SGCN and their habitats. SWAP element seven mandated by Congress in the development of each state's SWAP requires the lead agency to coordinate with "Indian tribes that manage significant land and water areas within the state or administer programs that significantly affect the conservation of identified species and habitats." There is one Native American tribe listed on the federal register in Mississippi --the Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians (MBCI). They own and manage almost 35,000 acres in several counties primarily in east-central Mississippi. The tribal biologist and representatives participated in activities related to the revisions, including webinars and email correspondence. Members of the Technical Committee met with tribal representatives to invite help and gather information and recommendations about culturally significant species that may also be SGCN. The Core Committee also presented an overview of the SWAP at the Mississippi Tribal Summit in 2023 which included tribal representatives from the MBCI as well as several tribes with cultural interests in Mississippi. A description of engagement with agency and tribal representatives is in Appendix 1.

div.head: Selection and Revision of Species of Greatest Conservation Need (SGCN)
div.p: The revision of the SGCN list for the 2025 SWAP involved reviewing and updating the information used to develop the previous lists. New information gathered on species was considered as well as any changes in State or Global ranks (according to NatureServe that assigns range wide or global status and status within the state -http://explorer.natureserve.org/nsranks.htm), federal or state threatened or endangered status, and other conservation status rankings. Experts throughout the state and region were consulted during this evaluation of the original list and the subsequent revisions. This evaluation of the original list resulted in the addition or removal of several species over the past 20 years. The current 2025 SGCN list was revised based on recommendations from the Southeast Association of Fish and Wildlife Agencies (SEAFWA) to improve the identification, assessment, and prioritization of SGCN using four priority tiers. See Appendix 10 for a description of the prioritization approach used to determine the 1060 SGCN in the 2025 SWAP. More information on ranks, tiers and the process of selecting SGCN can be found in Chapter 4.

div.head: Threats and Conservation Actions
div.p: The third element required by Congress in the development of the SWAP involves the description of problems that may adversely affect SGCN or their habitats. There are several different approaches noted in the literature, but most rely on identification of "stresses" or "threats" and/or "sources of stress" in the environment. The Best Practices for State Wildlife Action Plans (2012) recommends using the definitions and hierarchy found in the Salafsky et al. (2008) paper entitled A Standard Lexicon for Biodiversity Conservation: Unified Classifications of Threats and Actions. Creating consistency across state plans will make multi-state cooperation and projects easier to design by identifying shared threats and actions across states. The Technical Committee adopted Salasfsky's standardized classification of threats and actions and assigned a high, medium, or low rank to the identified threats to aid in determining the most critical problems for each identified habitat subtype and to facilitate identification of priority conservation actions. More information on threats and conservation actions associated with Mississippi's SGCN and their habitats can be found in Chapter 5 and Chapter 6.

div.head: Classifying Wildlife Habitats in Mississippi
div.p: Element two requires each state to produce "descriptions of locations and relative condition of key habitats and ecological community types essential to conservation of species identified as SGCN". To address this element in the first SWAP, experts responded to a detailed survey to identify and note the relative significance of the habitats and ecological communities for potential SGCN. Associating SGCN with their habitats and communities guided the process of prioritizing conservation actions to be taken. Targeting key habitats for conservation actions is often an effective way to ensure long-term survival of many SGCN. Prioritizing and implementing actions that protect, conserve or enhance habitats or communities shared by multiple SGCN should increase return on investments.

For 2025, Mississippi adopted the use of the EPA Level III and IV Ecoregions as a new geographic framework for presenting habitat classifications and incorporated for the first time the descriptions of NatureServe's Terrestrial Ecological Systems (TES) along with updated and refined the descriptions of habitat types and subtypes occurring in the state. Thus, for the 2025 SWAP, Mississippi is organized into four EPA ecoregions, and 19 major habitat types and 49 subtypes classified in the broad categories of terrestrial, major drainages, marine and estuarine, and artificial. See Chapter 5 for general descriptions and conditions for habitat types and subtypes located within the four EPA ecoregions of Mississippi. See Chapter 6 for the new Conservation Opportunity Areas.

div.head: Chapter 4 Selecting and Prioritizing Mississippi's Species of Greatest Conservation Need
div.p: The MNHP operates under the auspices of the MDWFP through the MMNS Bureau. It maintains a database of animals (vertebrates and invertebrates) and plants native to the state. To develop conservation priorities, each species is ranked according to the number of occurrences, population trends, and threats.

There are approximately 1,500 known species of animals in Mississippi which can be tracked by the MNHP, including all of the representatives of the groups gastropoda (snails); bivalvia (mussels); malacostraca (amphipods, crayfish, shrimp, isopods); arachnida (spiders, mites, ticks); insects; fish (including the cephalaspidomorphi -jawless fish/lampreys) and the osteichthyes (bony fish); amphibians (frogs and salamanders); reptiles (lizards, snakes, turtles, alligators); birds; and mammals. Tracking entails maintaining a database on occurrence localities, population status, and habitat conditions for tracked species. Many of the animals in the groups listed above are common, however, and are not tracked. Tracking is focused upon species known or suspected to occur in low numbers (with conservation rankings of S1 -Imperiled through S3 -Vulnerable including the borderline ranking of S3S4 -see Nature Serve Conservation Status ranking definitions below). These are designated as Species of Special Concern. There are 388 special concern animals, which include 8 gastropods, 53 bivalves, 34 crawfish and shrimp, 1 arachnid, 69 insects, 1 lamprey, 76 fish, 21 amphibians, 38 reptiles, 68 birds, and 19 mammals; and 658 special concern plant species, which include 32 non-vascular plants, 32 ferns and fern allies, 4 gymnosperms, and 589 angiosperms. An additional 153 plant species are designated as "watch" status.

div.head: Development of the Original SGCN: Historical Context
div.p: The initial SGCN list developed in 2005 for the first Mississippi SWAP was created from MDWFP's Animals of Special Concern and further evaluated by the SWAP Technical Committee and an Expert Team consisting of biologists with expertise relative to those species. These biologists assessed the ranks and provided extensive input via a formal survey regarding those ranks and the population status, species distribution, and habitat status. This original survey was sent to 81 individuals around the state and region, and 46 responded by completing 1,004 surveys. A similar survey was conducted to gather consistent data about each new species for the 2015 update. The original SGCN were sorted into four tiers to help determine the priorities for conservation actions. At the time, there was no national standardized method for states to follow in prioritization of the relative conservation needs of SGCN. Thus, the Technical Committee selected a set of criteria that can be applied objectively across the entire range of animal taxa included in this report (mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians, fish, crustaceans and mussels).

The Technical Committee elected to evaluate species based on seven relatively objective criteria that could be broadly applied. The original 2005 ranking system was based on seven criteria that included the NatureServe Global, National and State Ranks (See Appendix 6 for an interpretation of all NatureServe ranks), eligibility of species to receive funding, percent of population size or range in Mississippi, trend in population size, quality and quantity of available data and extent of known data about a species.

div.head: Development of the New 2025 SGCN List: Our Approach
div.p: For this 2025 SWAP update, the Technical Committee began with the prior SGCN list as the foundation, and applied a new set of criteria based on recommendations from the Southeastern Association of Fish and Wildlife Agencies' (SEAFWA) Wildlife Diversity Committee and their SWAP Standardization Subcommittee to state wildlife agencies in 2022. Our goal in revising the SGCN list for this 2025 iteration of the SWAP was to adopt a standardized approach taken by other states in the region to help us better implement conservation on a regional scale where warranted. The following is a summary of the approach we used to develop the SGCN list. We also added plant species for the first time. An explanation of how the first SGCN list of plants was developed is below.
The 2025 SGCN list is presented at the end of this chapter (Table 4.3). See Appendix 3 for a list organized by ecoregion and Appendix 8 for a list of the SGCN with their conservation rankings.

Steps to Updating the SGCN for 2025

The following are the data consulted and steps the Technical Committee followed to update Mississippi's SGCN list. The entire list and subsequent updates were distributed to an extensive group of experts, stakeholders, tribal representatives and other interested individuals in 2023 and 2024 and posted on the MDWFP website for public comment (See Appendix 2). Each comment was considered and the SGCN list adjusted where appropriate and justified. Refer to Appendix 6 for a detailed interpretation of the NatureServe Conservation Status Ranks.

1. SGCN Potential List. We began with the 2015 SGCN list for Mississippi with the understanding that some species could be added or removed during later stages of the revision. The list was supplemented with any additional species from the following groups: a. Endangered, Threatened, and Candidate Species currently listed by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service or the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. b. NatureServe -Critically Imperiled or Imperiled (G1-G2) species, including any species with rounded ranks within this range (i.e., G2G3 species and G1G3 species). G3 species are Vulnerable. c. Regional Species of Greatest Conservation Need (RSGCN) d. State Listed Species e. State Rarity Rank -Critically Imperiled or Imperiled (S1-S2) species, including any species with rounded ranks within this range (i.e., include S2S3 and S1S3 species). Species ranked SU (Unrankable), SH (Possibly Extirpated), and SX (Presumed Extirpated) should be considered on a case-by-case basis (see 2 below) f. USFWS at-risk species. g. International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) species ranked as Critically Endangered (CR), Endangered (EN), and (Vulnerable) VU. h. Partner's In Flight Category of Continental Importance: Red Watchlist, Yellow Watchlist, and Common Birds in Steep Decline.

2. Historic, Extirpated Species, and Uncertain species. Species ranked as SX (Extirpated) , SH (Historic), and SU (Unrankable) were considered on a case-by-case basis. Species that could potentially be rediscovered through additional surveys were included in the assessment. Similarly, species that are likely to be reintroduced or could recolonize restored habitats were considered for inclusion. Unrankable species that are potentially imperiled were considered.

3. Undescribed Species. If an undescribed species had strong evidence for inclusion, such as publications, reports that include genetic or morphological data, or recognition of the taxon by a professional society or conservation organization, we considered them.

4. Additional SGCN. Experts were asked for any additional recommendations such as recently described species, species with emerging threats or any other species with significant conservation needs that were not captured on the initial SGCN list.

div.head: Assessing Conservation Status.
div.p: Where state rarity ranks were not updated (within the last five years), we used the NatureServe ranking methodology to update state rarity ranks for potential SGCN.
6. Southeastern SGCN Database. We also consulted the Regional SGCN database.

7. Prioritize SGCN. After completing the species assessment using the steps and data above and garnering initial input from experts,we applied the SGCN priority tier reference guide to assign SGCN species to one of four priority levels: 1 -Highest Conservation Concern, 2 -High Conservation Concern, 3 -Moderate Conservation Concern, and 4 -Data Deficient. Species may merit prioritization by meeting any one of the listed reference criteria were included, but the prioritization was based on an overall synthesis of the priority tier definition and the most suitable criteria for assessing the status of a particular SGCN.

8. Deviations: Deviation from reference criteria was deemed appropriate for certain SGCN such as some migratory birds and species with very limited ranges in the state. Deviations from the above approach also included consideration of species with low population density, low reproductive potential and/or narrow geographic distributions that may not be included in endangered, threatened, imperiled or at-risk classifications (or are thought to be declining rapidly) and recommendations from experts (particularly with regard to the updates to the bird list, and the addition of marine species, insects, and plants).

Additionally, species identified as a conservation priority under national plans and peer-reviewed publications were considered for inclusion on the SGCN list. Examples of peer-reviewed publications which identify species as conservation priorities are: Partners In Flight North American Landbird Conservation Plan, U.S. Shorebird Conservation Plan, North American Waterfowl Management Plan, and the North American Waterbird Conservation Plan. Fish species identified as threatened or vulnerable by the American Fisheries Society and freshwater mussel species identified as endangered, threatened, or special concern by the American Fisheries Society were also considered. As noted above, some species on the MNHP's list of Animals of Special Concern were excluded from selection as SGCN. However, these animals will continue to be tracked by the NHP and may appear on future iterations of the SGCN.

div.head: New SGCN Priority Tiers
div.p: The Definitions for the 2025 SGCN priority levels are as follows. A table with the complete reference criteria considered for each level and explanation of the new approach based on the SEAFWA recommendations is in Appendix 10.

Tier 1 -Highest Conservation Concern: Critically imperiled species that may become extirpated from Mississippi in the near future unless conservation efforts are continued or enhanced. The population(s) in our state are very important to the global conservation of the species.Species that are in need of immediate conservation action and/or research because of extreme rarity, restricted distribution, unknown or decreasing population trends, specialized habitat needs and/or habitat vulnerability.

Tier 2 -High Conservation Concern: Imperiled species that may continue to decline in Mississippi unless conservation efforts are continued or enhanced. The population(s) in our state are important to the global or regional conservation of the species. Species that are in need of timely conservation action and/or research because of rarity, restricted distribution, unknown or decreasing population trend, specialized habitat needs or habitat vulnerability or significant threats.

Tier 3 -Moderate Conservation Concern: Species that may be currently stable but of long-term conservation concern due to increasing or emerging threats or species that are currently stable but are representative of an ecosystem or community in need of conservation or species that are currently stable but represented by a strong population or unique genetic diversity that is worthy of conservation within Mississippi. Species that are of less immediate conservation concern, but are in need of planning and effective management due to unknown or decreasing population trends, specialized habitat needs or habitat vulnerability.

Tier 4 -Data Deficient: Species that may be imperiled, but lack of information on their conservation status, taxonomy, life history, and threats precludes the identification of conservation actions. Species listed as extirpated from Mississippi, of historical occurrence only, or accidental. While no conservation action or research is recommended at this time, these species remain SGCN in the event that taxa may be rediscovered, reintroduced from populations existing outside the state, or are discovered to be regular, non-accidental components of the Mississippi's fauna.
Not SGCN: Species in this status category do not merit recognition as SGCN.

Not Applicable: This status category should not be used to prioritize SGCN for my taxonomic group because it may include species that do not merit SGCN or it may exclude species that do warrant SGCN status.

div.head: NatureServe Ranks For Animals Of Special Concern
div.p: Below is a summary of the Natureserve ranks referenced for the SGCN table below (state and global heritage ranks listed) and in the SGCN in Appendix 8. For a complete list of the NatureServe ranks, see Appendix 6.

Heritage Ranks: The MNHP uses the Heritage ranking system developed by The Nature Conservancy (http://explorer.natureserve.org/nsranks.htm). Each species is assigned a GRANK representing its range wide or global status and an SRANK representing its status in the state.

div.head: S1
div.p: Critically imperiled in Mississippi because of extreme rarity (5 or fewer occurrences or very few remaining individuals or acres of habitat) or because of some factor(s) making it vulnerable to extirpation.

div.head: S2
div.p: Imperiled in Mississippi because of rarity (6 to 20 occurrences) or because of some factor(s) making it vulnerable to extirpation.

div.head: S3
div.p: Rare or uncommon in Mississippi (21-100 occurrences).

div.head: S4
div.p: Widespread, abundant, and apparently secure in the state, but with cause for long-term concern.

div.head: S5
div.p: Demonstrably widespread, abundant, and secure in the state. SH Of historical occurrence in Mississippi, perhaps not verified in the past 20 years and suspected to be extant.

An element would also be ranked SH if the only known occurrence(s) were destroyed, or if it had been sought extensively and unsuccessfully looked for. Upon verification of an extant occurrence, SH-ranked elements would typically receive an S1 rank. SU Possibly in peril in Mississippi but status uncertain; need more information. May also be represented by S? S?

Unranked: Element is not yet ranked in the state. SX Element is believed to be extirpated from the state. SE Exotic: An exotic established in the state; may be native in nearby regions (e.g. pecans along the eastern seaboard of the US) SA Accidental: accidental or casual in the state (i.e. infrequent and far outside usual range). SNA Not Applicable: A conservation status rank is not applicable because the species is not a suitable target for conservation activities SP Potential: Element potentially occurs in the state but no occurrences reported. SR Reported: Element reported in the state but without persuasive demonstration which would provide a basis for either accepting or rejecting (e.g. misidentified specimen) the report. SRF Reported falsely: Element erroneously reported in the state and the error has persisted in the literature. HYB Hybrid: Element represents hybrid of species.

div.head: B = Breeding Status N = Non-breeding Status
div.p: Qualifiers: ? = Inexact C = Captive or Cultivated only GRANK: Criteria follow those of SRANK except for species having several subspecies. In these cases, a subrank, made up of the letter "T" plus a number or letter (1,2,3,4,5,H,U, X,?), is added to the GRANK.

div.head: STATE STATUS:
div.p: Eighty-six animals have been designated as state endangered through the Mississippi State Law, the Nongame and Endangered Species Conservation Act of 1974.
Plants receive no formal legal protection by state law in Mississippi other than that provided for in the trespass laws.

div.head: FEDERAL STATUS:
div.p: The following is a guide to acronyms taken from the Federal Register.

div.head: LE Endangered.
div.p: A species which is in danger of extinction throughout all or a significant portion of its range. LT Threatened. A species which is likely to become an endangered species within the foreseeable future throughout all or a significant portion of its range. PT Petitioned Species. A species for which a formal request has been made by the public or organization to the USFWS to evaluate its status and consider listing it as endangered or threatened. PP Proposed Species. A species that has been formally reviewed and determined to warrant listing as endangered or threatened but has not yet been finalized in the regulatory listing process.

PS Population Segment / Distinct Population Segment. The species or subspecies is listed in a portion of the population or range. The Distinct Population Segment is described geographically instead of biologically Adding Plants: Our Approach for the 2025 SWAP

In 2020, the Southeast Plant Conservation Alliance (SE-PCA) recognized the need for most states to integrate plant species into their SWAPs. In 2022, they paired with NatureServe, Terwilliger Consulting Inc, the Atlanta Botanical Garden, the Southeastern Association of Fish and Wildlife Agencies, and the Southeast Flora team to organize meetings with state and regional experts to create a list of plant species that were recognized as in need of conservation. The Southeastern Plants Regional Species of Greatest Conservation Need (RSGCN) list was completed in September 2023 and is the first plant RSGCN in the nation. The project started with NatureServe's Ranked Taxa list and determined a need for updated information for many species. A survey was sent to the state and regional experts, and this data was compiled into an initial list. Several meetings were held to finalize the list.
The NatureServe Ranked Taxa list selected species that:

1. A mode S-Rank of less than two within the region (with SH or SX equivalent to 0.5); 2. A G-Rank of G1, G2, G3, GH, or GX, or in some cases as G4 if at least five states ranked the taxon as S1, S2, SH, or SX and the taxon had at least 50% Regional Responsibility.
RSGCN were categorized as Very High, High, Moderate, and Low Level of Conservation Concern for ranking species.

div.head: RSGCN Conservation Ranks are defined as:
div.p: Very High: GX, GH, G1 (including G1G2, G1?), or G2 (including G2?)
High: G2 (including G1G3, G2G3) or G3 (including G3?) with only rounded S1, S2, SH, or SX state ranks
Moderate: G3 (including G3?) with SNR or rounded S3, S4 or other rounded G3 (including G2G4, G3G4) or G4 (including G4?) with more or less states with rounded S1, S2, SH, or SX state ranks

Low: G4 (including G3G5, G4?, G4G5), G5 (including G5?), or GNA Mississippi has 214 RSGCN of the 1,824 plant total species present on the regional list. Of these 13 are ranked Very High regionally, 20 are High, and 181 are Moderate. These species were used as the foundation of the state's plant SGCN list in the development of the 2025 SWAP. However, seven species were rejected as they were falsely attributed to Mississippi and 43 species were removed because they are not of conservation concern currently within the state (Table 4.2). Additionally, 384 species of vascular plants from the Mississippi Natural Heritage Program Special Plant Tracking List 2025 were added to the state SGCN list due to their rarity in the state if they had a Global Rank of G1, G2, G3, G3G4, or combinations of these global ranks, or a State Rank of S1, S2, or a combination of these state ranks. The decision was made to include 31 non-vascular plants that are recognized by NatureServe as rare to the Southeastern United States. SE-PCA is initiating a review of these species, but as of 2025 the project is still in development.
All plant species added to the SGCN list were placed in four tiers based on the same criteria as the existing animal list described above and detailed in Appendix 10.

div.p: Townes' Clubtail G3 S1 Within each level IV ecoregion, the SWAP Technical Committee paired the 38 primary terrestrial ecological systems in Mississippi described by NatureServe, which are based on the U.S. National Vegetation Classification (USNVC) and is the standard vegetation classification system for federal agencies (FGDC 2008). This approach was recommended by the Association of Fish and Wildlife Agencies (AFWA 2012) for regional and national consistency in the development of SWAPs and has been adopted for the development of Mississippi's 2025-2035 SWAP to align with surrounding state approaches.

The following is EPA's description of its Level III and Level IV ecoregions followed by a list of NatureServe's Terrestrial Ecological Systems (TES) that fall within each region and a list of Mississippi habitats. For a crosswalk of SWAP habitat types by TES, see Appendix 4.
Habitat descriptions, condition, status, maps and associated SGCN follow the presentation of EPA Ecoregions in this Chapter.

div.head: Southeastern Plains Ecoregion
div.p: Although mostly tree-covered, the Southeastern Plains are a mosaic of cropland, pasture, woodland, and forest land cover. Historically the southern region of this ecoregion was dominated by longleaf pine, with smaller areas of oak-hickory-pine and southern mixed forest. In central and northern Mississippi, oak-pine and some western mixed mesophytic forests were dominant. This region has higher elevations and relief than in the Southern Coastal Plain ( 75), but less than in much of the Piedmont. The streams of this region are relatively low-gradient and sandy-bottomed.There are ten level 4 subdivisions that occur in Mississippi in this ecoregion. 65a Blackland Prairie

The flat to undulating Blackland Prairie region is underlain by distinctive Cretaceous-age chalk, marl, and calcareous clays of the Selma group. The fine-textured, clayey soils tend to shrink and crack when dry and swell when wet. Streams are low gradient with chalk, clay, sand, and silt substrates, and have a high variability in flow which affects some fish species distributions. The natural vegetation had dominant trees of sweetgum, post oak, blackjack oak, and red cedar, along with patches of bluestem prairie. Today, the area is mostly cropland and pasture, with small patches of mixed hardwoods, red cedar, and pines. Pond-raised catfish aquaculture occurs in some parts of this region.

div.head: 65r Jackson Prairie
div.p: The Jackson Prairie ecoregion is a narrow belt of irregular plains and low, broad hills underlain primarily by the Yazoo Clay of the Eocene-age Jackson Group. The calcareous clay, sand, and marl is commonly overlain by alkaline, clayey soils that expand when wet and shrink when dry. Fossilized bones of ancient whale-like mammals (Basilosaurus cetoides and Zygorhiza kochii) are found in this formation, along with fossil oyster shells and other calcareous sediments that contributed to the formation of the alkaline soils. The historic vegetation was mostly mixed hardwood and pine forests with a scattering of prairies. The soils and gentle topography of the region attracted early settlement and agricultural development, but logging, cultivation, and land abandonment also caused extensive soil erosion. Fire suppression also allowed encroachment of woody vegetation into the prairies. Today, much of the region is forested or in pine plantations,

div.head: Mississippi Alluvial Plain Ecoregion
div.p: The Mississippi Alluvial Plain extends from southern Illinois, at the confluence of the Ohio River with the Mississippi River, south to the Gulf of Mexico. The broad, flat alluvial plain has areas of river terraces, swales, and levees providing the main elements of relief. Historically, deciduous bottomland forests dominated the region; much of it was cleared for cultivation and continues in this state today. There are five level 4 subdivisions that occur in Mississippi in this ecoregion.

div.head: 73a Northern Holocene Meander Belts
div.p: The Holocene floodplain of the Mississippi alluvial plain contains the meander belt of the present course of the Mississippi River and abandoned meander belts of its previous courses. Point bars, oxbows, natural levees, and abandoned channels are all characteristic of the Northern Holocene Meander Belts ecoregion. The meander belt is an alluvial ridge that is often at a higher elevation than the more distant floodplain or backswamp areas. The natural levees were the conspicuous landform of the meander belt, and their distribution influenced human settlements, transportation routes, and agricultural and industrial activities.

div.head: 73d Northern Backswamps
div.p: The Northern Backswamps ecoregion consists of flat, poorly drained, floodplain depressions where water often collects into small, low-gradient stream channels, lakes, swamps, and low-lying areas. These were areas generally not affected by lateral river-channel migrations. They often developed in areas of fine-grained overbank or slack-water deposits where sedimentation rates were relatively low. The soils are mostly gray to black and are clayey textured. Organic matter is locally abundant in the form of woody fragments, small particles, and peaty surface layers varying in thickness. Water levels are seasonally variable, and the clayey soils have high shrink-swell potential with periodic wetting and drying. Although there are a few small areas of bottomland hardwood forests, with cypress and tupelo in the wettest areas, large parts of this region in Mississippi are in cropland, farmed wetlands, pastureland, or contain large catfish ponds. The backswamps can be important areas for capturing excess nutrients from local waters and storing water during heavy rain events. Land cover is mostly loblolly and shortleaf pine forests or plantations, and forests have a higher concentration of pine than in the other regions of this ecoregion. Timber production occurs in the Homochitto National Forest and oil and gas production and exploration have been widespread in the region during the past fifty years. The eastern boundary of this region is broad, with a gradual transition to Ecoregion 65.

div.head: Terrestrial Ecological Systems included in this regionTerrestrial Ecological Systems included in this region
Southern Coastal Plain Ecoregion
div.p: The Southern Coastal Plain has a diversity of habitats including flat plains, barrier islands, coastal lagoons, marshes, and swampy lowlands along the Gulf and Atlantic coasts. This ecoregion is lower in elevation with less relief and wetter soils than the Southeastern Plains. Historically, the region had a variety of forest communities that included longleaf pine savannas, slash pine flatwoods, and southern mesic forests. Development has led to fragmentation of these communities. There are three level 4 subdivisions that occur in Mississippi in this ecoregion.

div.head: 75a Gulf Coast Flatwoods
div.p: In Mississippi, the Gulf Coast Flatwoods is a narrow region of nearly level terraces and delta deposits composed of Quaternary-age sands and clays. Wet, sandy flats and broad depressions that are locally swampy are now usually forested or in pine plantations, while some of the better-drained land has been cleared for pasture or crops. Dominant land uses include woodland, wildlife habitat, and urban. Historically, pine savannas with slash and longleaf pine and a variety of grasses, sedges, rushes, pitcher plants and orchids were common. A high natural fire frequency was typical, often sparked by lightning and fueled by wiregrass that maintained the more open savannas.
Terrestrial Ecological Systems included in this region:

div.head: Marine Habitats (Outside the Barrier Islands) -No Ecoregion Equivalent
div.p: Marine habitats of the Mississippi Gulf Coast occur in the region beyond the barrier islands within the western third of the Mississippi-Alabama continental shelf. Nearshore and offshore regions of the shelf are roughly two million acres in size. The shelf extends southward along a gradual sloping plain of unconsolidated sand, muddy sand and mud substrates for a distance of approximately 100 miles. It gradually deepens from the shallows off the barrier islands to a depth of 600 feet along the outer continental shelf.
There is no TES equivalent. The two habitat types included in the SWAP under Marine habitats are Hard Bottom and Smooth Bottom.

div.head: Habitats in Gulf Barrier Islands and Coastal Marshes
div.p: Artificial Reefs; Hard Bottoms and Oceanic Reefs; Mississippi Sound (Smooth Bottom).

div.head: Classifying Wildlife Habitats in Mississippi
div.p: Within the four Level III ecoregions that occur in the state, Mississippi has 19 overarching habitat types organized by four systems: terrestrial, freshwater streams, estuarine and marine and artificial. Each is further subdivided into subtypes and cross walked with NatureServe'sfoot_0 Terrestrial Ecological System (TES) classifications where there is an equivalent.

Element Two of the eight required elements to be addressed in SWAPs requires each state to produce "descriptions of locations and relative condition of key habitats and ecological community types essential to conservation of species identified as SGCN". To originally address this element, experts were enlisted through survey instruments and input to identify and note the relative significance of the habitats and ecological communities for potential SGCN. Associating SGCN with their habitats and communities guided the process of prioritizing conservation actions to be taken. Targeting key habitats for conservation actions is often an effective way to ensure long-term survival of many SGCN. Prioritizing and implementing actions that protect, conserve or enhance habitats or communities shared by multiple SGCN should increase return on investments.

In the past, the Mississippi Natural Heritage Program (MNHP) Ecological Community List was simplified and incorporated within the SWAP to expedite the process of associating SGCN with their habitats and communities. The MNHP list includes 159 natural, semi-natural, managed, weedy and probable subtypes which have been assigned conservation priority ranks indicating their relative endangerment or abundance.

For the purposes of this plan, the 159 ecological community types used in the MNHP were matched to the 38 International TES listed by NatureServe as occurring in Mississippi. The following table lists the habitats which are generally organized on the basis of land type, vegetation and the availability of moisture (by ecoregion). A few MNHP ecological community types have no equivalent in the NatureServe TES; these are noted in the chapters and the tables for each habitat type where applicable.

Each habitat type includes a map showing the general location of the habitat subtypes (where mapping is possible), and a brief description of the type, condition and an estimate of the extent and conservation status followed by a list of SGCN associated with each subtype. Note that the maps presented are not a visual representation of habitat to scale.

div.head: TERRESTRIAL HABITATS
div.p: Table 5.2 below lists all terrestrial habitat types and subtypes and their equivalent within NatureServe's TES classification as the Level III EPA Ecoregion where they occur. Following the table is a summary description of each habitat type, and subtype and NatureServe TES (where there is an equivalent). The extent, condition and a list of SGCN for each habitat type are also included. Dry forests are often found on well-drained soils of upper slopes and flats and include mixed hardwood and pine forest associations. Fire played an important role in maintaining these habitats by reducing densities of young saplings, recycling nutrients and oxidizing ground litter.
Several culturally significant species utilize this habitat including hickories, oaks, white-tailed deer, and squirrels.

div.head: General Condition
div.p: Although there are no estimates of the losses of Dry Mesic Upland Forests/Woodlands in Mississippi, it is possible to envisage their overall condition by understanding the extent of development pressure generated on these habitats. Historically, large areas of upland hardwood and pine forests were converted to agricultural croplands and pasture. The tracts were selected from the areas containing the most productive landforms and soils. Most landforms of the coastal plain are not excessively steep or isolated and are therefore accessible to either timber management or agricultural usage. Due to a history of pine monoculture and fire suppression, typical upland forests lack a diverse understory and exhibit very high stem densities. Upland forests of Mississippi benefit from prescribed burning, but timing of prescribed burning is an important issue: to most closely approximate the condition of the historic forests, burns should occur in late spring and early summer, when natural ignitions were most likely and when litter moisture was low enough to facilitate fire propagation. With an increased interest in conservation, through sustainable forestry practices such as the single tree select cut system of timber harvesting, and a renewed interest in forest restoration on private and public lands, conditions of these forests may improve.

Shortleaf pine historically dominated upper slopes and droughty ridge tops along watershed boundaries in the northern half of the state. Naturally occurring loblolly pine existed in pine and mixed hardwood-pine stands on moist upland flats, mid/lower slopes of drainageways and high stream terraces in areas merging with the longleaf pine region and extending through central and northern Mississippi. Post oak, blackjack oak, scarlet oak and hickory, along with other hardwoods, were commonly mixed with the pine on the drier sites with shortleaf pine often mixed with loblolly pine. Loblolly pine contributes more than 40 to 100 percent of the tree cover on lower slopes and flats. Hardwoods, including southern red oak, post oak, white oak, upland laurel oak, blackgum and sweetgum, are mixed with pine on better sites and make up about 80 percent of the subcanopy. Magnolia, shortleaf pine, tuliptree, hickories, oaks and other trees represent the remaining 20 percent. Longleaf pine forest historically covered most of the southern portion of the state, extending from slightly above today's I-20 corridor south to I-10. The area typically featured a rolling topography of very well drained soils. Nested within the piney woods were hillside seepage slopes of pitcherplants. Fires maintained forests and savannas of massive, well-spaced longleaf pine trees. Combustible leaf litter and grassy understory carried natural wildfires through the longleaf region. Sampling of virgin forests over a century ago indicated that tree densities averaged about 100 per acre, or 400 square feet per tree. With the wider spacing of trees, ample sunlight was able to reach the forest floor and support a diverse cover of herbaceous plants. Species richness is high in this community with 150 to 300 species per hectare found on the richest fire-maintained sites with shrubs, grasses and forbs, accounting for one-third of the ground cover. Mesic longleaf forests once formed an extensive blanket across the uplands of the piney woods region but were logged during the last two centuries. Second growth forests, many of which were converted to other pines, now occupy the undulating hills and plains of the region.

Because of the current emphasis on timber production, many existing longleaf pine stands are even-aged and have much higher stocking densities. Although significant land conversion has occurred, longleaf forests are common on national forest lands and some private holdings. East Gulf Coastal Plain Northern Dry Upland Hardwood Forests occur in a limited portion of northern Mississippi and includes the Northern Pontotoc Ridge. These dry hardwood forests occupy dry upland slopes and ridge tops with nutrient poor soils of various textures. Characteristic species of this community are oaks (post, southern red, blackjack and white) and hickories (mockernut and sand). Shortleaf and loblolly pines are commonly intermingled with the hardwoods. The rare chestnut oak slope and ridge forests are mainly found in the northeastern corner of the state, where the steep slopes are underlain by limestone, shale, and chert beds of the Carboniferous formation.

div.head: Southern Coastal Plain Dry Upland
div.p: Hardwood Forests consist of deciduous or mixed evergreen oak-dominated forests, often with pines present. These occur within a landscape dominated historically by pines and occurred in fire-sheltered locations on dry to dry-mesic soils in naturally small to large patches. Sites are somewhat protected from most natural fires by steep topography and by limited flammability of the vegetation. Forests in the northern range in the state may have been more widespread. Darlington's oak is a typical species in many examples, with post oak, southern red oak, and white oak less frequently encountered, but dominant in some stands. Hickories, other hardwood tree species, and pines will be present. Stands may be found on slopes above rivers and adjacent to sinkholes, as well as other fire-infrequent habitats including narrow bands between mesic slopes below and pine-dominated flats above. The soils are generally well-drained but not excessively drained.

div.head: Southern Coastal Plain Oak Dome and Hammock is an isolated community in South
div.p: Mississippi. The canopy is usually dominated by live oak. Fires rarely burn through this community due to the limited fuel source; winter burning regimes may have allowed this type to expand in what may have been longleaf pine dominated woods. The soil and moisture conditions vary from dry to more mesic. In addition to the live oaks, Darlington's Oak, sand live oak, bluejack oak, turkey oak, and sand post oak may be present.

div.head: East Gulf Coastal Plain
div.p: Interior Shortleaf Pine-Oak Forests form one of the largest communities in the Southeastern Plain of Mississippi. These gently rolling uplands were found on well-drained clays or sandy soils with dry to dry-mesic moisture. Shortleaf pine dominated the region historically but have been replaced by loblolly pines through much of the former range. Hardwood trees are present in more mesic areas and include several oaks (white, southern red, blackjack, and post oaks) and mockernut hickory. Natural fires influenced the composition of the community, with shortleaf pines having difficulty regenerating in the absence of fire.

div.head: Size, Condition and Conservation Status
div.p: Dry Mixed Hardwood and Pine Forests: Many tracts containing this forest subtype have been converted to cultivated forests for pine production. Very few forests of this subtype are managed with prescribed burns. Where fire management is used, there is a significant reduction in the density of shrubs and small trees and an improvement in herbaceous ground cover. Ridgetops are used for transportation corridors and the secondary development that is associated with roads. Dry hardwood forests are highly fragmented and considered to be in poor condition due to complete exclusion of fire, which allows off-site bottomland species to invade uplands, altering forest composition. Few stands are known to be in good condition and few are protected from conversion to other uses. Continuation of these threats unabated will likely lead to additional declines.

Dry Pine Forests: Increased stocking densities and lack of fire has decreased the quality of this extensive and widespread subtype. Some mature stands are managed by thinning and controlled burns. These thinned stands have a more productive ground cover and prove more valuable for wildlife. Many of the better managed stands are found in state wildlife management areas. Natural stands of dry-mesic shortleaf/loblolly pine forests are found in small and large patches throughout the central and northern part of Mississippi. Shortleaf pine forests are usually found in smaller patches on narrow ridgetops. The pine stands are interspersed with plantations, cutover areas and hardwood stands. East Gulf Coastal Plain Interior Upland Longleaf Pine Woodland is the dominant community in south Mississippi. Longleaf pine would have been the most characteristic canopy tree, but many stands have been altered by a long history of exploitation, harvest, and stand conversion, primarily to agriculture or cultivated forests of slash pine or loblolly pine. Soil and moisture conditions range widely in this community, from excessively well-drained to mesic soils. Natural fires suppressed most hardwood tree species. Dry longleaf pine communities are found on upper slopes and ridge tops, and may have turkey oak, sand post oak and bluejack oak mixed in the canopy. Saw palmettos are also usually present. In areas with high clay content soils, blackjack oak may become more abundant. Turkey oak-sand post oak woodlands are a highly altered longleaf pine community, from which the longleaf pines were harvested sometime in the past. This community occurs on sandy caps of hill crests or on thick deposits of sand in floodplain terraces. Small regenerating longleaf pines may be found at the edges. Attempts to establish loblolly pine plantations were common in the past, but usually these failed and the remaining trees are stunted. Mesic longleaf pine communities are more widespread than dry longleaf pine forests in Mississippi. Dry longleaf pine forests are found in upland areas that have loamy soils over clay or clay loam soils on a relatively level to gently sloping plain. The soils are moist, periodically wet, but droughty also. Towards the south part of the region, slash pine is more common with increases in other species going north through the region. Common associates are post oak, blackjack oak, southern red oak, mockernut hickory, white oak, red maple, sweetgum, water oak and upland laurel oak. In these forests, little bluestem and slender bluestem grasses are the most obvious components of the herbaceous layer. Several culturally significant species utilize this habitat including hickories, yaupon holly, white-tailed deer, and squirrels.

div.head: Size, Condition and Conservation Status
div.p: Size: Estimated 1.23 million acres of Longleaf Pine Forest

div.head: Conservation Status: Critically Imperiled to Imperiled
div.p: The upland sites that support longleaf pine forests have been used for road corridors, sand sources and homesites. Fire suppression and conversion to other land uses, including pine plantations, have caused serious qualitative and quantitative declines of this community. While many stands are pure longleaf pine, loblolly and slash pine are common in others. In some stands not managed with fire, dense shrub and vine thickets, reaching six to fifteen feet in height, will shade out the normally rich assemblage of herbs. If left unaltered, this community succeeds to an oak-hickory-pine community on drier sites and to beech-magnolia in mesic areas. Only a fraction of the original forest remains (about three percent). Some large tracts of this subtype are found in the De Soto National Forest and a few private holdings. Many sites in the piney woods have been converted to commercial timber production and are typically planted in off-site species such as loblolly or slash pine. Tracts supporting this subtype range up to 10,000 acres in size (such as the area surrounding White Plains), but many tracts are much smaller.

div.head: Threats and Actions for Dry-Mesic Upland Forests/Woodlands
div.p: Threats: Modification of these habitats to cultivated forests are the primary threat to these communities. Other significant threats are fire suppression, poorly timed prescribed burns, and invasive species.

Actions: Encourage retention, preservation, and conservation of remaining natural habitat through purchase, easements or MOAs. Encourage and improve management of habitat by controlled burning at necessary frequencies and seasons. Limit/discourage the introduction of propagation of exotic and invasive species. Control/eradicate such species when present. Promote and develop landowner incentive and assistance programs for conservation of SGCN and their habitats. Provide public education about the conservation of SGCN and/or their habitats.
