figure.figDesc: The Prairie Grasslands COA includes Level 4 ecoregions of 65a, 65r, and the western portion of 65b and covers 23 counties. Prairies are dominated by warm season perennial grasses, maintained by regular fires. These fires were historically set by Native American Indians or dry season lightning strikes. Today prescribed burns are used as a management tool. The Mississippi Forestry Commission's Forest Legacy Program (2020) North Forest Legacy Area covers some portion of this COA in the Blackland Prairie (65a) ecoregion and the Central Forest Legacy Area lies over the western portion of the Jackson Prairie (65r) ecoregion. Sixty-six HUCs are found in this COA that are designated as high priority for conservation of SGCN.

row.cell: Conservation Sites in the Prairie Grasslands COA
• Sam D. Hamilton Noxubee National Wildlife Refuge
• John W. Starr Wildlife Management Area

note.p: 7.4. Prairie Grasslands Conservation Opportunity Area.

figure.head: Table 7 .5. Important Habitats in Prairie Grassland COA
figure.figDesc: Historic threats to Prairie Grasslands were in the form of conversion, either to urban/suburban areas or to crop/pastureland. Current threats include lack of proper fire regimes, overgrazing and row-crop agriculture. Multiple invasive species are an issue in this COA, with two of the worst plant invaders being kudzu and Chinese privet. Others include wild hogs, fire ants, Asian carp, exotic mussels, and numerous aquatic invasives.

figure.head: Table 7 .6. Prairie Grassland Species of Greatest Conservation Need.
Alluvial Plain Conservation Opportunity Area Figure
figure.figDesc: The Mississippi Alluvial Plain COA aligns with the Level 3 ecoregion 73. It covers all or parts of 33 counties. It is a region of broad, flat alluvial plain with river terraces, swales, and levees as the main elevations. Historically, the predominant habitat in the South Delta region was forests, primarily hardwoods. Today, the major land use is private cropland and grasslands. Main crops are cotton, soybeans, milo, and corn. Catfish and crawfish are produced commercially on farm ponds in this COA. Seventy-seven HUCs are found in this COA that are designated as high priority for conservation of SGCN.

row.cell: There are opportunities to protect land around these conservation sites.
Conservation Sites in the Mississippi Alluvial Plain COA

note.p: ThreatsThreats to the Loess Bluffs COA are similar to other parts of the state. Urban and suburban development, fragmentation, and forest conversion pose a threat to all of the habitats within this COA. Channel modifications that cause erosion and headcutting and sand/gravel mining are impacting the streams and rivers, and the SGCN within them. Multiple invasive species are an issue in this COA, with two of the worst plant invaders being kudzu and Chinese privet. Others include Cherokee rose, wild hogs, fire ants, Asian carp, exotic mussels, and numerous aquatic invasives. For a more complete list of threats refer to specific habitats listed above in Chapter 5.

Flatwoods Conservation Opportunity Area Figure
figure.figDesc: The Coastal Flatwoods COA is the Level III ecoregion 75 on the mainland of Mississippi and covers three coastal counties. An important aspect of this COA is the role it plays in maintaining the health and diversity of the Mississippi Sound. Near the Gulf Coast, drainage areas are low-lying flatlands, forested wetlands, and marshlands. This COA is found in the Mississippi Forestry Commission's Forest Legacy Program (2020) Southeast Mississippi Forest Legacy Area. Thirty-eight HUCs are found in this COA that are designated as high priority for conservation of SGCN.

figure.figDesc: Information available from the Mississippi GAP Analysis Program, Aquatic GAP, the Mississippi Automated Resource Information Center (MARIS), USGS, the Mississippi Department of Marine Resource's Coastal Resource Management Program (CRMP), NatureServe, the Southeast Conservation Blueprint, Southeast Conservation Adaptation Strategy (SECAS), and others can be used to track landscape changes over time. These programs are especially valuable for remotely assessing the status of private lands. Although programs provide a strong foundation for tracking habitats, further refinement to mapping and GIS capabilities is needed to meet SWAP long-term goals. Land cover information must be updated periodically to be useful in tracking long-term changes.Because the SWAP is a statewide strategy developed to provide guidance to facilitate conservation on all public and private lands. Inclusion of monitoring activities performed by all public and private individuals and entities is essential. Information from the Landowner Incentive Program (LIP), Farm Bill conservation programs such as the Conservation Reserve Program (CRP), Agricultural Land Easement Program (ALE), the Wetland Reserve Easement Program (WRE) and the Wildlife Habitat Incentives Program (WHIP), Ducks Unlimited (DU) and the Joint Ventures partnerships, the Forest Legacy Program and others such as The Nature Conservancy's Conservation Area Partnerships that facilitate conservation practices should provide indications of success action on private lands. Organizations and agencies such as the NRCS and the USDA Farm Services Agency (FSA), Mississippi Forestry Commission (MFC), the Mississippi Soil and Water Conservation Commission (MSWCC) and Wildlife Mississippi work closely with landowners and can be valuable resources for assessing accomplishments on private lands. Several lands trusts have also been established in the state and can provide information related to private lands.

figure.figDesc: the association level generally is the classification unit assessed and ranked (see Classification of Ecological Communities at www.natureserve.org for an explanation of the classification hierarchy). Only global conservation status ranks are currently available for ecological communities on NatureServe Explorer. The primary factors for assessing community status are: Species known in an area only from historical records are ranked as either H (possibly extirpated/possibly extinct) or X (presumed extirpated/presumed extinct). Other codes, rank variants, and qualifiers are also allowed in order to add information about the element or indicate uncertainty. See the lists of conservation status rank definitions for complete descriptions of ranks and qualifiers.

figure.figDesc: Unranked -Global rank not yet assessed. value, or of domestic origin. For ecosystems, the type is typically non-native (e.g. many ruderal vegetation types), agricultural (e.g. pasture, orchard) or developed (e.g. lawn, garden, golf course). Distinctiveness of this entity as a taxon or ecosystem type at the current level is questionable; resolution of this uncertainty may result in change from a species to a subspecies or hybrid, or inclusion of this taxon or type in another taxon or type, with the resulting taxon having a lower-priority (numerically higher) conservation status rank. The "Q" modifier is only used at a global level and not at a national or subnational level. abundant than the species, for example, a G1T2 subrank should not occur. A vertebrate animal population (e.g., listed under the U.S. Endangered Species Act or assigned candidate status) may be tracked as an infraspecific taxon and given a T rank; in such cases a Q is used after the T-rank to denote the taxon's informal taxonomic status. Species or ecosystem is believed to be extirpated from the jurisdiction (i.e., nation, or state/province). Not located despite intensive searches of historical sites and other appropriate habitats, and virtually no likelihood that it will be rediscovered. [equivalent to "Regionally Extinct" in IUCN Red List terminology] Known from only historical records but still some hope of rediscovery. There is evidence that the species or ecosystem may no longer be present in the jurisdiction, but not enough to state this with certainty. At a fairly low risk of extirpation in the jurisdiction due to an extensive range and/or many populations or occurrences, but with possible cause for some concern as a result of local recent declines, threats, or other factors.Range Rank -A numeric range rank (e.g., S2S3 or S1S3) is used to indicate any range of uncertainty about the status of the species or ecosystem. Ranges cannot skip more than two ranks (e.g., SU is used rather than S1S4). SGCN Potential List. Consider specific groups of species as potential SGCN at the beginning of the revision process, with the understanding that some species could be added or removed from the SGCN list during later stages of the revision. The potential list should start with the current 2015 SWAP list of SGCN for your state or territory. The list should then be supplemented with any additional species from the following groups: a. Endangered, Threatened, and Candidate Species currently listed by the U.S.Fish and Wildlife Service or the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.b. NatureServe G1-G2 species, including any species with rounded ranks within this range (i.e., include G2G3 species and G1G3 species). c. Regional Species of Greatest Conservation Need d. State Listed Species e. NatureServe S1-S2 species, including any species with rounded ranks within this range (i.e., include S2S3 and S1S3 species). f. U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service at-Risk species. The USFWS defines 'at risk species' as species that are petitioned, a candidate or proposed for listing under the U.S. Endangered Species Act. While this category overlaps partly with item a, the at-risk finder is useful for identifying these species in your state or territory. g. IUCN Red list species ranked as CR (critically endangered), EN (endangered), and VU (vulnerable) at the global scale of assessment. h. Partner's In Flight Category of Continental Importance: Red Watchlist, Yellow Watchlist, and Common Birds in Steep Decline.

Infraspecific Taxon Global Conservation Status Ranks RA NK DEFINITION T# Infraspecific Taxon (trinomial) -The status of infraspecific taxa (subspecies or varieties) are indicated by a "T-rank" following the species' global rank. Rules for assigning T-ranks follow the same principles outlined above. For example, the global rank of a critically imperiled subspecies of an otherwise widespread and common species would be G5T1. note.p: GNANot Applicable -A conservation status rank is not applicable because the species or ecosystem is not a suitable target for conservation activities. A global conservation status rank may be not applicable for several reasons, related to its relevance as a conservation target. For species, typically the species is a hybrid RANK DEFINITION without conservation Q Questionable taxonomy that may reduce conservation priority -CCaptive or Cultivated Only -Taxon or ecosystem at present is presumed or possibly extinct or eliminated in the wild across their entire native range but is extant in cultivation, in captivity, as a naturalized population (or populations) outside their native range, or as a reintroduced population or ecosystem restoration, not yet established. The "C" modifier is only used at a global level and not at a national or subnational level. Possible ranks are GXC or GHC. This is equivalent to "Extinct in the Wild (EW) in IUCN's Red List terminology(IUCN 2001).

figure.head: Priority tier reference guide that may be used to help assign SGCN to priority tiers.
figure.figDesc: Assessing Conservation Status. Coordinate with your state's NatureServe Program Office (NSPO) to obtain the most recent rarity ranks for species you are including in your assessment. If state rarity ranks have not been recently updated (within a few years), work with your NSPO to update rarity ranks using the NatureServe ranking methodology. The SWAP revision process is a good opportunity to engage experts and organize the data needed for ranking. If existing NSPO staff are not completing the ranking, provide opportunities for your staff or species experts to participate in an upcoming training session. Keep in mind that experts can override the rank calculator with sufficient justification. Further, it is preferable to determine an SU rank (unrankable) when NatureServe ranking factors are poorly estimated.7. Southeastern SGCN Database. Utilize the Southeastern SGCN databasedeveloped by the subcommittee to complete your species assessment. The database will include standard terminology, threats, NatureServe ranking factors, and conservation actions and will be available on or before October 1 st , 2022. If your state already has an SGCN database that it prefers to use, consider adopting data fields and definitions included in the SGCN database where feasible. An additional document describing the database is in preparation. 8. *Prioritize SGCN. After completing the species assessment, utilize the SGCN priority tier reference guide (Table 1) to assign SGCN species to one of four priority levels: Highest Conservation Concern, High Conservation Concern, Moderate Conservation Concern, and Data Deficient. If species do not meet any of the reference criteria, think carefully about whether they should be designated as SGCN. A species may merit prioritization by meeting any one of the listed reference criteria. However, prioritization should be based on an overall synthesis of the priority tier definition and the most suitable criteria for assessing the status of a particular SGCN. Deviation from reference criteria may be appropriate for certain SGCN. 9. *Document Your Process. Describe the process you used to identify, evaluate, and prioritize SGCN within your SWAP so that your results are clearly understood and repeatable. Please document any deviations from the recommendations presented in this document. Critically imperiled species that may become extirpated from my state in the near future unless conservation efforts are continued or enhanced. The population(s) in my state are very important to the global conservation of the species.

note.p: NatureServe, Inc. is a non-profit organization that provides proprietary wildlife conservation-related data, tools, and services to private and government clients, partner organizations, and the public. They maintain the National Vegetation Classification Standard for the United States as well as the International Classification of Ecological Communities, currently focused on the Western Hemisphere.
-Data Deficient Species that may be imperiled, but lack of information on their conservation status, taxonomy, life history, and threats precludes the identification of conservation actions.

div.head: Tables
div.p: Table E There are opportunities to protect land around these conservation sites. Additionally, Bayou Pierre, White Oak Creek, Big Black River, upper Yalobusha, Amite River, Yockanookany River, Clark Creek, and their tributaries have been highlighted as targets for conservation. The Piney Woods COA includes the lower Pascagoula River and Pearl River Basins and covers all or parts of 33 counties. It extends south from the Jackson Prairie ecoregion 65r and east of the Southern Rolling Plains ecoregion 74c. The Piney Woods COA is heavily forested throughout, primarily of pine with scattered hardwoods. The topography consists primarily of gently rolling hills and broad, flat floodplains. The Pascagoula River supplies a large portion of the freshwater entering the sound. In so doing, it replenishes nutrients and sediments that play a critical role in maintaining the productivity of the coastal waters. The Pearl River is one of the most intact river systems in the Southeast U.S. with a great diversity of wildlife species and habitats (TNC 2001). A relatively natural, unlevied system, it supports a large number of SGCN. Wetland systems within this COA provide invaluable ecosystem functions such as controlling erosion, absorbing excess nutrients and helping to reduce flooding. The lower Pearl River supports one of the healthiest marsh complexes in the Southeast (TNC 2004) Additionally, areas around Red Creek, Black Creek, Pearl River, Pascagoula River, and their tributaries are of high priority for conservation. The Devil's Backbone is an area of conservation interest along the border of Marion/Pearl River Counties east of Hwy 43. Ragland Hills north of Highway 98 near Ragland, MS is an area of beech-magnolia bluff forest and is utilized by SGCN.

div.head: Tribal Nations
div.p: As sovereign conservation partners, Tribes should be included in SWAP revisions and implementation, particularly for any decision-making that affects their interests (Schmidt et al., 2023). Meaningful engagement with Tribes requires demonstrated respect for their individual Tribal sovereignty, as well as their history, culture, and governmental structure. During the development of this 2025 SWAP update, MDWFP coordinated with representatives of the MBCI and representatives of other federally recognized Tribes with cultural interests in Mississippi to discuss identification of SGCN that are also culturally significant species. In these discussions, we learned that conservation priorities for Tribal Nations may differ from those determined to SGCN for the purposes of the SWAP. Culturally significant species may be defined as species that have been or are still currently utilized by a tribe, either for subsistence (food or income), medicinal uses, and cultural preservation (arts and ceremony). In a step toward incorporating culturally significant species into the SWAP we are including the following list of culturally significant species that are available for public knowledge (provided by the MCBI and the NAFWS representatives). We acknowledge that some culturally significant species are private knowledge of the tribe, and some tribal knowledge has been lost. Thus, the following list is not a comprehensive list, but rather a starting point. Over the next ten years we wish to increase collaboration with the Tribes to help them develop a SWAP for their conservation priorities, such as a stand-alone document or for incorporation into the next iteration of Mississippi's SWAP. We also commit to seeking opportunities for continued collaboration on conservation efforts such as prescribed fire, continuation of bioassessments on tribal lands and restoration of culturally significant species such as Swampcane and Switchcane. Our Technical Committee worked with other scientists around the state and region with expertise on SGCN and their habitats to help compile and synthesize the data for review and input. A Core Committee of MDWFP managers ensured the process followed Congressional guidelines and met the eight required elements. Plan updates were posted on the MDWFP website for public review and input over a three year period (2023 -2025) for continued stakeholder and public input and refinement as plan elements were updated.

During the 2025 revision process, stakeholders communicated primarily via email, and through individual and small group or professional meetings and submitted comments through the SWAP page on the MDWFP website. Public and stakeholder input was gathered through:
• A Mississippi SWAP page on the MDWFP website (www.mdwfp.com).

• Media alerts announcing the SWAP update and changes as updates sections were released on the agency website and social media platforms. • Multiple invitations to stakeholders to comment on SWAP elements as they were drafted. • Presentations at professional conferences, tribal and science meetings.
• Individual meetings in person and online.

The first SWAP was developed in 2005 with coordination with committees (Technical, Steering and Advisory Committees) and a team of Expert Advisors and public input. Since the first SWAP was approved, Mississippi's SWAP Technical Committee and experts continued to work together through meetings and informally to build on the original body of work for the 2015 and 2025 SWAP updates. The following are lists of the committee members instrumental in the 2025 update. 2025 MS SWAP Core Team -Aaron Holbrook, Emily Rezac, Heather Sullivan, Quentin Fairchild and Liz Barber served to organize the feedback, write, edit and compile the 2025 update and organize meetings and input from the inhouse Technical Committee and outside experts and stakeholders. Other collaboration with bordering states and other SWAP coordinators occurred primarily during national and regional meetings hosted by the Association of Fish and Wildlife Agencies (AFWA) and through the development and update of the Regional SGCN list. The addition of the plants for the first time in this 2025 SWAP was done in coordination with the Southeastern Association of Fish and Wildlife Agencies' development of Regional SGCN of Southeastern Plants.

div.head: Interpreting NatureServe Conservation Status Ranks
div.p: Conservation Status Ranks are referenced for the SGCN lists in Chapter 4 and the descriptions of conditions for each habitat subtype in Chapter 5. Below is an explanation of these terms.

The conservation status of a species or community is designated by a number from 1 to 5, preceded by a letter reflecting the appropriate geographic scale of the assessment (G = Global), N = National, and S = Subnational/State). The numbers have the following meaning: To make the best use of federal funds from the WCRP and SWG program, Congress mandated each state and territory to develop a SWAP to guide conservation investments at the state level. In the authorizing legislation, Congress identified eight required elements to be addressed in each state's SWAP and directed that the plans must identify and be focused on the Species of Greatest Conservation Need (SGCN) yet address the full array of wildlife and wildlife-related issues.
Below is a list of the eight required elements and the chapters and appendices where each element is addressed in this 2025 SWAP update:

Required Element 1: Species -Information on the distribution and abundance of species of wildlife, including low and declining populations as the state fish and wildlife agency deems appropriate, that are indicative of the diversity and health of the state's wildlife.
(Chapters 4, 5, 7, Appendix 3, 8).
Required Element 2: Habitats -Descriptions of extent and condition of habitats and community types essential to conservation of species identified in (1). (Chapters 4, 5, Appendix 5).

Required Element 3: Threats -Descriptions of problems which may adversely affect species identified in (1) or their habitats, and priority research and survey efforts needed to identify factors which may assist in restoration and improved conservation of these species and habitats. (Chapters 5,6,7,8,Appendix 11,12).

Required Element 4: Conservation Actions -Descriptions of conservation actions proposed to conserve the identified species and habitats and priorities for implementing such actions. (Chapters 5,6,7,8,Appendix 11).

Required Element 5: Monitoring Species and Effectiveness -Proposed plans for monitoring species identified in (1) and their habitats, for monitoring the effectiveness of the conservation actions proposed in (4), and for adapting these conservation actions to respond appropriately to new information or changing conditions. (Chapter 8, Appendix 12).
Required Element 6: Review and Revision -Descriptions of procedures to review the plan at intervals not to exceed ten years. (Chapter 9).

Required Element 7: Partnerships with Land Management Agencies and Tribes -Plans for coordinating the development, implementation, review, and revision of the plan with federal, state, and local agencies and Indian tribes that manage significant land and water areas within the state or administer programs that significantly affect the conservation of identified species and habitats (Chapter 9, Appendix 1 and 2).

Required Element 8: Public Participation -Broad public participation is an essential element of developing and implementing these plans, the projects that are carried out while these plans are developed, and the species in greatest need of conservation (Appendix 1 and 2).
